messages.content: What is the freezing point point of water at a pressure of 10 kPa?

message.content:
**Freezing point of pure water at 10 kPa**

| Pressure | Approximate freezing point |
|----------|----------------------------|
| **10 kPa** | **–0.005 °C to –0.010 °C** |

---

### How this was obtained  

Water’s melting/freeze‑point line has an almost flat slope with respect to pressure because the volume change when ice melts is very small compared with its latent heat.  
Using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation for the ice↔water transition,

\[
\frac{dP}{dT}= \frac{\Delta H_{\text{fusion}}}
                    {T\,\Delta V},
\]

with

* \( \Delta H_{\text{fusion}}\approx 6.0\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\)
* \( \Delta V \approx -1.6\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^{3}\,mol^{-1}}\)
* \( T\simeq 273\,\mathrm{K}\),

yields

\[
\frac{dP}{dT}\;\approx\;-1.4\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{Pa\,K^{-1}}
          \quad(\text{i.e., }-14\,\mathrm{MPa/K})
\]

A decrease of pressure from atmospheric (\(~101.3\) kPa) down to 10 kPa changes the temperature only by

\[
\Delta T=\left(\frac{dT}{dP}\right)\!\Delta P
        \approx-\frac{1}{14\,\mathrm{MPa}}\times90.3\,\mathrm{kPa}
        \approx-0.0065\,^\circ\mathrm{C}.
\]

Hence the freezing point drops by less than one hundredth of a degree Celsius—essentially staying at 0 °C for all practical purposes.

> **Bottom line:** Water freezes at essentially 0 °C even under a vacuum of 10 kPa; the theoretical shift is only about ‑0.007 °C.
